newsitem.title: USA: Ariz. county okays proposed settlement with SEC.
newsitem.headline: Ariz. county okays proposed settlement with SEC.

text.p: Maricopa County, Ariz., supervisors on Wednesday approved a proposed settlement with the Securities and Exchange Commission over charges of securities fraud in connection with $48 million of bonds.

Earlier this week, the SEC alleged that Maricopa County, the nation's sixth largest county, violated the anti-fraud provisions of federal securities laws in connection with the July 1993 sale of two series of general obligation bonds by failing to disclose that county finances had deteriorated.
Separately, SEC officials in Los Angeles said they have settled securities fraud charges against financial adviser Peacock, Hislop, Staley & Given Inc. over the county bonds.

As part of the settlement, the Phoenix-based firm agreed to pay $50,000 in fines and partner Larry Given agreed to $25,000 in fines for their involvement in the bond deals. Under the terms of the deal, the firm neither admitted nor denied any of the SEC's findings.
Robert Casillas, a senior vice president with the firm, said the settlement was appropriate.
"Our settlement, without admitting or denying the commission's findings, was the prudent course of action for our business and our clients," Casillas said.

"As a small regional firm, the settlement of this matter avoids the huge costs which would be associated with having an ultimate determination of the merits of the SEC's case by the judicial system," Casillas said.
Maricopa County's five-member county Board of Supervisors approved the settlement offer by a vote of 4-to-0, with one supervisor abstaining from the vote due to a conflict of interest.

The settlement offer must still be approved by the Securities and Exchange Commission. The county, which includes the city of Phoenix, said it expected the settlement to be accepted by the SEC shortly.

The county said the terms of the settlement were prepared in collaboration with attorneys for the SEC. Under the settlement, the county agrees not to violate securities laws in the future but neither admits nor denies any of the SEC's allegations. No fines or penalties will be imposed.
County supervisors approved the proposed settlement at their meeting in Phoenix with little discussion.
"We don't believe it will have any effect on the county's future financings," said Joe Duke, a county attorney.
Some municipal finance experts contend that settlements with the SEC would increase a municipality's borrowing costs.

The SEC action against Maricopa County was precedent setting because it was the first action by the commission against a general purpose issuer of municipal bonds where the securities were not in default.
The Maricopa County case was also the first major SEC action in the municipal bond market since its settlement with then-bankrupt Orange County, Calif., in January.
